enrichment.short_title: Gencon charterparty signature determines owner party to arbitration
key_facts: A Gencon voyage charter for the Elikon named Sphinx Navigation c/o Internaut Shipping as owner, but Internaut signed unqualified under the owners signature box.
Demurrage arbitration was commenced in 1995 and conducted for years in the name of Sphinx, although Internaut had instructed solicitors and Gard.
The court was asked who was party to the charterparty, who was claimant in the original arbitration, and whether the tribunal could substitute Internaut for Sphinx in the pleadings.
The Court of Appeal held Internaut, not Sphinx, was the owner party to the charterparty and the original arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from declarations on charterparty and London arbitration party issues ordered for trial by Cresswell J.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on issues (1) and (2); issue (3) varied so arbitration conducted in Sphinx's name was a nullity but the original Internaut arbitration survives.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party signs a charterparty in its own name without qualification under the owners signature box, it is prima facie personally liable as owner unless the body of the contract clearly shows otherwise; naming Sphinx elsewhere did not rebut that, and the misnaming of Sphinx in later arbitration pleadings was not a mere misnomer but left the valid Internaut arbitration still in being.
legal_issues: Construction of a Gencon charterparty to identify the owner party
Effect of an unqualified signature under the owners signature box
Whether Sphinx or Internaut was party to the original London arbitration
Whether arbitrators had power to substitute Internaut for Sphinx in the points of claim

enrichment.short_title: Quarter costs awarded after Law Society concession on penalty challenge
key_facts: Mr Haycocks challenged a Law Society disciplinary penalty by judicial review and appeal.
The Law Society made a helpful concession on the point on which the court was anxious, giving Haycocks another opportunity to challenge the penalty.
The court considered Haycocks' conduct before and during proceedings, including lateness and poor engagement with the disciplinary process.
Although the court had provisionally indicated no order for costs, it awarded Haycocks one quarter of his costs here and below.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on costs following successful challenge to a Law Society disciplinary penalty.
enrichment.outcome: Appellant awarded one quarter of his costs here and below, including the costs of the appeal day, to be assessed if not agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR Part 44 the court may depart from costs following the event by reference to parties' conduct and success on issues; even where a claimant's conduct was poor, a modest costs award may be justified where proceedings were necessary to obtain relief the defendant ultimately conceded.

Effect of a defendant's concession on the 'event' for costs purposes

enrichment.short_title: No Article 2 duty to fund family representation at hospital death inquest

statutes_considered.title: Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997
Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Three-year-old Naazish Khan died at St James Hospital, Leeds in October 1999 after a catastrophic potassium infusion error during treatment for B-cell lymphoma.
Police, NHS and CPS investigations followed; the hospital later admitted liability and an inquest was due.
The claimant sought a declaration that the Secretary of State must fund legal representation for the family at the inquest or a public inquiry.
The Secretary of State argued Article 2 was not engaged because the death preceded the Human Rights Act 1998 and existing investigations had already satisfied any investigative duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review after permission was granted on the papers.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed: Article 2 investigative duties already complied with, no obligation to fund legal representation at the inquest, and in any event Article 2 was not engaged because the death occurred before the Human Rights Act came into force.
enrichment.ratio: The Article 2 duty to investigate deaths in hospital is adjectival and dependent on the substantive Article 2 right being engaged at the time of death; where adequate independent investigations and admission of liability have occurred, family participation and state-funded legal representation at an inquest are not invariably required, and the adjectival duty cannot arise for deaths before 2 October 2000.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 required funding of legal representation at an inquest
Whether the state had already complied with Article 2 investigative obligations
Whether Article 2 was engaged where the death occurred before the Human Rights Act 1998 came into force
Whether the Secretary of State had power to fund representation under the NHS Act 1977

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Two linked appeals challenged social security rules under the Human Rights Act 1998.
Reynolds concerned lower jobseeker's allowance and income support rates for claimants aged 18 to 24 than for those aged 25 or over.

Carson concerned the exclusion of certain UK pensioners living abroad, mainly in Old Commonwealth countries, from annual pension uprating paid to pensioners in the UK and selected other jurisdictions.

enrichment.short_title: Murder convictions quashed after police misconduct and prejudicial hearsay
key_facts: Poole and Mills were convicted in 1990 of murdering Hensley Wiltshire after a fight in Gloucester.
The prosecution depended heavily on Kimberley Stadden and, to a lesser extent, Paul White; eyewitness Juke did not give evidence.
Police misconduct included a false witness statement by White, DI Gladding's intimidation of Juke, and prejudicial hearsay from Juke's statement put to Mills in interview.
The CCRC referred the case after the Divisional Court expressed doubt about safety; this was the second Court of Appeal hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal against conviction on reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; both murder convictions quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Convictions may be unsafe where non-disclosure prevented the defence testing an important eyewitness and where critical, inaccurate hearsay from an absent witness was left before the jury on central issues; following Pendleton, the court must focus on safety rather than guilt and may assess how fresh irregularities would reasonably have affected the jury.
legal_issues: Whether DI Gladding's misconduct tainted the whole prosecution
Effect of non-disclosure about Paul White's account to the police
Prejudicial hearsay use of Juke's witness statement in police interviews
Application of R v Pendleton to reassessing witness credibility and jury impact

confidence.notes: Extremely detailed judgment with explicit reasons for allowing both appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Youth Court may reinstate stayed proceedings under section 22B

statutes_considered.title: Prosecution of Offences (Youth Courts Time Limits) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Two young defendants faced robbery charges in the Croydon Youth Court under statutory time limit regulations.
The Youth Court extended the overall time limit, but the Crown Court on appeal refused the extension and the proceedings were stayed.
The Chief Crown Prosecutor reinstituted proceedings by laying fresh informations in the Youth Court under section 22B.
The district judge held reinstatement was invalid because the Crown Court had stayed the proceedings, so only indictment in the Crown Court was permitted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review of a Youth Court decision declining jurisdiction over reinstituted proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: DPP's application allowed; district judge's decision quashed and fresh proceedings directed to proceed to trial in the Croydon Youth Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where Youth Court proceedings are stayed because an overall time limit expires, a Crown Court decision on an extension appeal substitutes for the Youth Court's order and does not itself become the staying court; fresh summary proceedings may therefore be reinstituted in the Youth Court under section 22B(3)(b) by laying an information.

Whether section 22B(3)(a) or (b) governs reinstatement after a refused extension appeal
Effect of section 110 Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 on appellate substitution
Exercise of discretion to direct reinstatement despite delay

enrichment.short_title: Murder conviction quashed where pathologist evidence on time of death withheld
key_facts: Trevor Wickens was convicted in 1991 of murdering 89-year-old Mrs Crandell at Herne Bay.
The prosecution case rested on alleged confessions to ex-wives and acquaintances; timing of death was central to undermining those accounts.
At trial the pathologist evidence was presented as neutral on whether death occurred on the Saturday night confessed to or the following Sunday afternoon.
On CCRC reference, Professor Vanezis gave fresh evidence that death on the Saturday was extremely unlikely, which the jury had not heard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following CCRC reference under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and murder conviction quashed; prosecution did not seek retrial.
enrichment.ratio: A conviction is unsafe where the Crown's own pathologist would have told the jury that the confessed time of death was extremely unlikely; applying Pendleton, the court cannot treat such expert evidence as neutral when it would materially have affected the jury's assessment of confession evidence.
legal_issues: Whether non-disclosure of police/pathology documents affected fairness
Significance of fresh expert evidence on rigor mortis and time of death
Impact on safety of treating pathological evidence as neutral in the summing up
Application of Pendleton to expert evidence appeals

confidence.notes: Full judgment with detailed analysis of pathological evidence and explicit quashing of the conviction.

enrichment.short_title: Part 36 uplift interest concession does not trigger indemnity appeal costs
key_facts: Ali Reza-Delta succeeded on appeal in a shipping dispute, increasing damages from US$115,800 to US$227,400.
The court had already awarded indemnity costs of the trial after earlier Part 36 offers beaten at trial.
A third Part 36 offer made during the appeal offered to accept US$227,400 plus indemnity trial costs but waived uplift interest on damages and costs.
The appellants sought indemnity costs of the appeal under CPR 36.21 or, alternatively, CPR 44.3.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further costs argument following substantive shipping appeal judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Respondents ordered to pay appellants' costs of the appeal on the standard basis only.
enrichment.ratio: Following Mitchell v James, concessions as to uplift interest in a Part 36 offer are ancillary matters and are not part of the sum for which a defendant is held liable or the judgment obtained for CPR 36.21 purposes; matching the principal sum alone does not engage the indemnity costs consequences of rule 36.21 on appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a Part 36 offer waiving uplift interest can trigger CPR 36.21 indemnity costs on appeal
Whether Mitchell v James applies to interest concessions as well as costs concessions
Whether indemnity costs of the appeal should be awarded under CPR 44.3

confidence.notes: Focused costs judgment with clear reasoning and order on standard-basis appeal costs.

enrichment.short_title: Elvis Costello photograph copyright retained by photographer against record label
key_facts: Chris Gabrin photographed Elvis Costello and other Stiff Records artists in 1977 for a publicity shoot.
Stiff Records paid up to £50 for publicity use but paid separate fees and acquired copyright when photographs were used on record sleeves.
Barney Bubbles later created a silk-screen print from the Costello photograph for sale on the Stiff tour.
Universal used the screen-print image on a 1999 CD booklet; Gabrin claimed infringement of his copyright in the photograph and jointly in the screen-print.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of copyright infringement and title defences.
enrichment.outcome: Gabrin established ownership of copyright in the photograph and infringement by use in the screen-print; claim to joint copyright in the screen-print failed for lack of proof of letters of administration; estoppel defence rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Publicity photo shoots reimbursed for expenses and a modest fee did not amount to a section 4(3) commission where Stiff only acquired copyright when it paid the higher record-sleeve fee; an agreed licence for promotional use of a screen-print did not extend to use on a CD booklet, and title to the screen-print copyright was not proved without a grant of administration.
legal_issues: Whether the 1977 shoot was a commission under Copyright Act 1956 section 4(3)
Whether Gabrin retained copyright in publicity photographs not bought for record sleeves
Ownership of copyright in Barney Bubbles' screen-print
Whether Universal was estopped from relying on Gabrin's earlier acquiescence

enrichment.short_title: Invalid care allowance restored from incapacity benefit cessation date

statutes_considered.title: Social Security and Child Support (Decisions and Appeals) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mr Adams cared for his disabled partner and was entitled to invalid care allowance from 1995, but payment was suppressed while higher incapacity benefit was paid.
The Department terminated his incapacity benefit on 12 May 2000 but failed to resume invalid care allowance until March 2001 when Adams reported the change.
The Secretary of State treated the March 2001 decision as a section 10 supersession and refused backdating to May 2000.
The Social Security Commissioner held payment should have resumed from 12 May 2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal to the Court of Appeal against a Social Security Commissioner's decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; invalid care allowance payable from 12 May 2000 and the ex gratia payment treated as made as of right.
enrichment.ratio: Where an award of invalid care allowance already exists and overlapping benefit rules merely adjust payment while incapacity benefit is paid, resumption after incapacity benefit ends is a section 8 decision on an existing entitlement rather than a backdated section 10 supersession; the Department cannot rely on the claimant's failure to notify what the Department already knew from its own cessation decision.
legal_issues: Whether resumption of invalid care allowance was a section 8 or section 10 decision
Whether payment could be backdated to the date incapacity benefit ceased
Effect of regulation 4 Overlapping Benefits Regulations on continuing entitlement
Whether the claimant had a duty to notify the Department of cessation of incapacity benefit
